result: Neutrophils are the predominant phagocyte responsible for clearing apoptotic hepatocytes through a novel mechanism termed 'perforocytosis,' where neutrophils burrow directly into apoptotic hepatocytes and ingest them from the inside. This was demonstrated through multiple microscopy techniques in human and mouse liver samples, showing neutrophils (up to 22 per apoptotic hepatocyte in humans, average of 2 in mice) penetrating and clearing apoptotic hepatocytes within 4-7 minutes without causing inflammation or tissue damage.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states this is a 'fundamental discovery of a new function of neutrophil' and calls it a 'solid study.' Reviewer 2 notes 'experiments were well designed and conducted' and confirms the visualization of perforocytosis. Reviewer 3 provides 'strong evidence that neutrophils can remove apoptotic hepatocytes in vivo and in vitro' and states 'the authors have provided reasonably strong evidence for the conclusion that neutrophils burrow into apoptotic hepatocytes to perform perforocytosis.'

result: Neutrophils show cell-type specificity in their phagocytic activity, clearing apoptotic hepatocytes but not apoptotic endothelial (HUVECs) or epithelial (HEK293) cells. Macrophages showed lower phagocytic capacity for apoptotic hepatocytes compared to neutrophils.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this finding, stating 'neutrophils are involved in removal of apoptotic hepatocytes with certain specificity (i.e., they do not remove HEK293 or HUVEC endothelial cells).' No reviewer challenges this specificity data, and it is presented as supporting evidence for the novel role of neutrophils.

result: Apoptotic hepatocytes release specific signals (IL-1β and IL-8) and express selectins that attract neutrophils and mediate perforocytosis. Knockdown of IL-1β receptor abolished phagocytosis, while IL-8 receptor knockdown reduced it by 50%, and selectin inhibition abrogated neutrophil-mediated clearance.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges the study explored 'signals/mechanisms' and notes this would be 'of great clinical significance' for future work, implicitly accepting the mechanistic findings presented. No reviewer challenges the signaling data, and the experiments are described as 'well designed and conducted' by Reviewer 2.

result: Neutrophil depletion in mice causes defective removal of apoptotic hepatocytes (0.92% vs 0.2% in controls, p<0.001), induces tissue injury with impaired liver function (increased AST, ALT, and bilirubin), and leads to compensatory macrophage activation. These effects were specific to liver and not affected by antibiotic treatment.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'neutrophil depletion impairs the clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes causing impaired liver function,' directly affirming these findings. Reviewer 3 notes the evidence suggests 'this neutrophil-mediated efferocytosis process keeps the number of apoptotic cells low in the livers,' accepting the depletion results. No reviewer challenges the experimental design or conclusions from the depletion studies.

result: Neutrophil depletion leads to generation of autoantibodies (anti-SMA, anti-ANA, anti-LKM, total IgG) in mice, suggesting defective neutrophil-mediated clearance contributes to autoimmune liver disease genesis. This effect was not observed with macrophage depletion or affected by antibiotic treatment.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms 'generation of autoantibodies, implying a role of defective neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic cells in Autoimmune Liver disease.' Reviewer 3 states 'defects in the processes may associate with autoimmune liver (AIL) disease phenotypes,' accepting this connection. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'transforms the way we think about role of neutrophil in pathogenesis of autoimmune liver disease.'

result: Human autoimmune liver disease patients show defects in neutrophil-mediated clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes. AIL patient samples contained apoptotic hepatocytes not phagocytosed by neutrophils, with more macrophage association. AIL neutrophils showed markedly decreased phagocytic ability and reduced expression of IL1R1 and PSGL-1 receptors compared to normal controls.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges 'evidence is provided to suggest that this neutrophil-mediated efferocytosis process keeps the number of apoptotic cells low in the livers and that defects in the processes may associate with autoimmune liver (AIL) disease phenotypes.' All reviewers accept the connection to autoimmune disease without challenging the human patient data.

result: Neutrophils possess a specialized immunologically silent mechanism for clearing apoptotic hepatocytes through perforocytosis. Despite up to 22 neutrophils entering a single apoptotic hepatocyte, there was little detectable tissue injury or inflammation, suggesting neutrophil recruitment does not always induce tissue damage.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states neutrophils clear apoptotic hepatocytes 'without causing inflammation as a part of tissue homeostasis.' Reviewer 2 confirms neutrophils ingest cells 'from inside without causing inflammation.' No reviewer challenges the claim that this process is immunologically silent, and all accept it as a key feature of the mechanism.

result: The study reveals a fundamental mechanism for removal of effete hepatocytes, demonstrating that neutrophils contribute to tissue homeostasis beyond their traditional role in immune surveillance. Defects in this housekeeping function may have implications for pathogenesis and treatment of autoimmune diseases.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 calls this a 'fundamental discovery' that 'transforms the way we think about role of neutrophil.' Reviewer 3 states 'many of these findings are novel and the study is of important implications in our understanding of the role of neutrophils in autoimmune disease.' All reviewers accept the broader significance of the findings for understanding neutrophil biology and disease.

result: Neutrophils are ideally suited for swift clearance of apoptotic hepatocytes due to their abundance (up to 70% of white blood cells), and the 'eating inside' mechanism provides a novel way to maintain liver integrity by preventing leakage of toxic contents. Macrophages show compensatory activation when neutrophils are depleted.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'neutrophils are the most abundant circulating leukocytes in human' and accepts their role in apoptotic clearance. The compensatory macrophage activation is implicitly accepted as part of the depletion study results that all reviewers affirm. No reviewer challenges the functional significance or the compensatory mechanism.
